questions.q: Define the oxygen dissociation curve and state the percentage saturation of haemoglobin at a pO₂ of 100 mm Hg under normal physiological conditions.
questions.a: The oxygen dissociation curve is a sigmoidal graph plotting percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against partial pressure of oxygen (pO₂). At pO₂ = 100 mm Hg (alveolar capillary), haemoglobin is approximately 97–98% saturated. A wrong answer (e.g., 100% saturation or a linear curve) reveals the student has not grasped the asymptotic nature of the curve or the concept that 100% saturation is never fully reached at physiological pO₂.

questions.q: Explain why the oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic, linking your answer to the molecular structure of haemoglobin.
questions.a: The sigmoidal shape arises from positive cooperativity: binding of the first O₂ molecule to one subunit of the haemoglobin tetramer induces a conformational change (T → R state) that increases the affinity of the remaining three subunits for O₂. A hyperbolic curve would indicate non-cooperative binding (like myoglobin). If a student says "haemoglobin has four binding sites so it binds four O₂", they miss the cooperative mechanism — the key is that affinity changes with each binding event.

questions.q: A person ascends to high altitude (3500 m) where atmospheric pO₂ drops to 90 mm Hg. Predict the effect on arterial oxygen saturation and explain the physiological compensation that occurs over days.
questions.a: Arterial pO₂ falls to ~60 mm Hg, moving onto the steep part of the curve; saturation drops from ~97% to ~89% (approx 8% decrease). Over days, increased 2,3-BPG in RBCs shifts the curve rightward, further lowering affinity to enhance tissue unloading, while hyperventilation raises alveolar pO₂ slightly. A wrong answer that claims saturation remains unchanged or that the curve shifts left reveals confusion between acute hypoxemia and chronic adaptation.

questions.q: Compare the oxygen dissociation curves of adult haemoglobin (HbA) and fetal haemoglobin (HbF) at the same pO₂. Which has higher affinity and why is this advantageous for the fetus?
questions.a: HbF has higher oxygen affinity (curve shifted left) because its γ-subunits bind 2,3-BPG less strongly than β-subunits of HbA. This allows oxygen to diffuse from maternal blood (lower affinity) to fetal blood (higher affinity) across the placenta. A student who says "fetal curve is right-shifted" confuses the direction of shift and fails to understand the transplacental gradient.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "During vigorous exercise, the Bohr effect reduces oxygen loading in the lungs because increased CO₂ and H⁺ shift the curve rightward."
questions.a: The statement is partially incorrect. In the lungs, hyperventilation blows off CO₂, lowering pCO₂ and raising pH, which shifts the curve leftward — enhancing loading. The rightward shift occurs in tissues where CO₂/H⁺ are high, promoting unloading. A student who agrees completely misunderstands that the Bohr effect is spatially compartmentalized: left shift in lungs, right shift in tissues.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a spectrophotometer to demonstrate the effect of pH on oxygen binding to haemoglobin. Specify the wavelength, samples, and expected absorbance changes.
questions.a: Use 540 nm (isosbestic point for Hb/HbO₂) or dual-wavelength (e.g., 577 nm for HbO₂). Prepare haemoglobin solutions at pH 7.4 and pH 7.2, equilibrate with air (21% O₂), measure absorbance. Lower pH sample will show lower HbO₂ absorbance (right shift). A poor design omits temperature control, uses non-physiological pH, or ignores that CO₂ must be controlled separately to isolate pH effect.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Transport of oxygen in human blood occurs primarily through reversible binding to haemoglobin (Hb) in red blood cells, forming ______ (HbO₂); each Hb molecule binds up to four O₂ molecules, and the sigmoidal oxygen dissociation curve describes the relationship between partial pressure of oxygen (pO₂) and percentage saturation of haemoglobin, which is shifted by pCO₂, H⁺ concentration (Bohr effect), and temperature to facilitate loading in alveoli and unloading in tissues.
Fill in the blank: Notice how your fingers turn pale when pressed and pink again when released — that's ______ loading and unloading oxygen in real time.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can draw and label the oxygen dissociation curve, explain the physiological significance of its sigmoidal shape, predict direction of curve shift given changes in pCO₂/pH/temperature, and calculate oxygen delivery per 100 mL blood using the arteriovenous oxygen difference.
